headline_en: Seven men and women rescued from traffickers' den in Teknaf, three detained
summary_en: The Coast Guard rescued seven men and women from a traffickers' hideout in the hills of Baharchhara, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, on the night of Sunday 7 December 2025; they had been brought there to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea. Men were lured with job promises and women with marriage promises, then held while the traffickers tried to extort money. Three men were detained with a local-made firearm.

facts.statement: Seven men and women from the Jaliapalong area of Ukhiya upazila were brought to a traffickers' hideout in the deep hills of Baharchhara, Teknaf upazila, Cox's Bazar, to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea; the Coast Guard rescued them in a raid on the night of Sunday 7 December 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Coast Guard, Lieutenant Commander Salauddin Rashid Tanvir

facts.statement: According to the Coast Guard (Lt Cdr Salauddin Rashid Tanvir, 8 December 2025), traffickers lured men with promises of jobs and women with promises of marriage to take them to Malaysia by sea, then held them captive at the Baharchhara hideout in Teknaf and tried to extract money from them.
facts.source_in_article: Lieutenant Commander Salauddin Rashid Tanvir, Coast Guard

facts.statement: In the Baharchhara, Teknaf raid of 7 December 2025 the Coast Guard detained three men with a local-made firearm on trafficking charges: Abdur Rahman (32) and Hamid Hossain (28) of Marishbunia village, Baharchhara union, and Helal Uddin (30) of neighbouring Baro Deil village; legal action was in process as of 8 December 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Coast Guard press conference at Kerontoli, Teknaf

facts.statement: The Coast Guard said on 8 December 2025 that such raids to stop human trafficking by sea (from the Teknaf coast to Malaysia) will continue.

headline_en: Campaign in London to encourage expatriates to register as voters
summary_en: The Election Commission is letting Bangladeshis abroad vote by postal ballot in the coming national election for the first time. In London, the group Policy for Good Governance campaigned in Newham to help Bangladeshis register on the EC app, and the Bangladesh High Commission is publicising the process. UK registration runs 29 November to 3 December via the 'Nagorik' app using NID, passport number and UK address.

facts.statement: Prothom Alo (November 2025) puts the number of Bangladeshis living outside Bangladesh at 1.5 to 2 crore (15 to 20 million).
For the first time, Bangladeshis living abroad can vote in the coming national parliamentary election by postal ballot, under an Election Commission initiative (reported November 2025).
Bangladeshis and British-Bangladeshis living in the UK could register for postal voting on the Election Commission app for five days, from 29 November to 3 December 2025.

To register for postal voting from the UK: download the Election Commission's 'Nagorik' app on a smartphone, enter NID details, passport number and UK address; after verification, if the EC accepts the request, a ballot paper is sent by post, and the filled ballot must be returned by post within the set time.

Eligibility for expatriate postal-vote registration (EC, November 2025): Bangladeshi by birth or descent, with a valid passport or NID on record; proof of current address abroad is required, and anyone already a voter must update the same information.

The Bangladesh High Commission in London is publishing infographics, video tutorials and messages on postal-vote registration on its website, Facebook page and other digital channels; press minister Akbar Hossain said they had done so for four days and would involve expatriate organisations.
facts.source_in_article: Akbar Hossain, press minister, Bangladesh High Commission London

facts.statement: On Sunday 23 November 2025 the group Policy for Good Governance, led by coordinator Mahbuba Jebin, handed out leaflets at Green Street and Stratford station in Newham, east London, and helped passers-by download the EC app and register; it had held a seminar 'Voting from abroad' on 14 November and plans to campaign in other UK cities with many Bangladeshis.

UK BNP held a press conference on 15 November 2025 on expatriate voting and instructed every unit to get leaders, workers, family members, relatives and neighbours registered for postal vote in time, said its office secretary Mujibur Rahman; expatriates told the reporter that political parties had otherwise done little.
facts.source_in_article: Mujibur Rahman, UK BNP office secretary

headline_en: How many mobile phones can returning travellers bring duty-free
summary_en: Under the Baggage Rules (non-tourist), a passenger returning from abroad may bring one new mobile phone and two used phones duty-free; extra new phones are taxed BDT 5,000 to 25,000 by price. The article lists the 19 duty-free items and 11 dutiable items allowed under the rules, including a 117-gram gold bar for BDT 40,000 duty.

facts.statement: Under Bangladesh's non-tourist Baggage Rules (as reported November 2025), a passenger returning from abroad may bring one new mobile phone and two used mobile phones duty-free; additional new phones are taxed.

Per the NBR customs wing (November 2025), duty-tax on each extra new mobile phone brought by a returning passenger is BDT 5,000 for a phone priced up to BDT 30,000, BDT 10,000 for BDT 30,000-60,000, and BDT 25,000 for over BDT 60,000; the maximum tax on a phone is BDT 25,000.

Under the Baggage Rules, 19 types of goods can be brought duty-free and 11 types on payment of duty: duty-free items include two used and one new mobile phone, a carpet up to 15 square metres, a TV up to 29 inches, a desktop or laptop, computer scanner, printer, video camera, still or digital camera, oven and microwave, rice cooker, pressure cooker, gas oven, toaster, sandwich maker, blender, food processor, juicer, coffee maker, sewing machine, table fan, sports goods for personal use, 100 grams of gold jewellery, one carton of cigarettes, and a music system with CD and speakers.

Under the Baggage Rules, a returning passenger can bring a 117-gram gold bar on payment of BDT 40,000 duty-tax; other dutiable items are a 234-gram (20 tola) silver bar, TVs of 30 inches or more, home theatre, refrigerator and deep freezer, air conditioner, dish antenna, HD camera, chandelier, an air gun with Commerce Ministry permission, and dishwasher, washing machine or clothes dryer, with duty ranging from BDT 300 to BDT 90,000.
Because of restrictions on bringing phones under the Baggage Rules, many phones enter illegally; the BTRC wrote to the NBR recommending lower duty on mobile phone imports (reported November 2025).

headline_en: Anti-Bangladesh campaign in Portugal: expatriates angered by André Ventura billboard
summary_en: A billboard of Chega party leader André Ventura reading 'Is to no Bangladesh' ('This is not Bangladesh') near a bus stop in Montijo, Portugal, angered Bangladeshi expatriates. Chega, the main opposition party, is campaigning on an anti-immigration platform ahead of the January 2026 presidential election. A Bangladeshi community leader said the matter had reached the Bangladesh embassy and government.

facts.statement: In October 2025 a political billboard near a bus stop in Montijo, Portugal, showed Chega party leader André Ventura with the slogan 'Is to no Bangladesh' ('This is not Bangladesh'), part of Chega's anti-immigration campaign ahead of the January 2026 presidential election; Bangladeshi expatriates called it insulting.

Chega, led by André Ventura, is described as Portugal's main opposition party and is campaigning on an anti-immigration stance; political analysts quoted say the slogan is used to stir anti-immigrant feeling and negative views of South Asian, especially Bangladeshi, workers.

Shahid Ahmed (Prince), general secretary of the Bangladeshi organisation 'Casa do Bangladesh' in Portugal, said the billboard had come to the notice of the Bangladesh embassy and government and the community wants a diplomatic solution.
Portuguese citizens' reactions to the billboard were mixed: some backed it as reflecting anti-immigration reality, many condemned it as hateful and shameful.

headline_en: Security being increased at key installations
summary_en: After three major fires in Dhaka and Chattogram, including at the Shahjalal airport cargo village on 18 October 2025, the home ministry's core committee decided to tighten security at key installations. Home Adviser Jahangir Alam Chowdhury also said the government had decided to cut passport fees for migrant workers to a reasonable level and is trying to improve Biman's service.

facts.statement: Home Adviser Lt Gen (retd) Jahangir Alam Chowdhury said on 20 October 2025 that a decision has been taken to reduce passport fees for migrant workers ('remittance fighters') to a reasonable level; no new fee amount was given.

The Home Adviser said on 20 October 2025 that migrant workers often do not get the respect or good service they deserve, that they usually try to travel on Biman Bangladesh Airlines because they understand the language and can eat home food, and that efforts are under way to improve Biman's service quality.

A major fire broke out at the cargo village of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on 18 October 2025; a 12-member committee headed by Home Secretary Nasimul Gani was formed to investigate and report by 5 November 2025.

headline_en: 'The debt remains, and my son has left the world'
summary_en: Md. Habib Khan, 21, from Matlab Dakshin, Chandpur, went to Saudi Arabia in November 2023 on a 'free visa' through a Narayanganj broker after borrowing 5.5 lakh taka. After a short spell at a residential hotel in Mecca he found little work and little pay under a local broker, and died in a Mecca hospital after a heart attack. His family is waiting for the body and the debt is unpaid.

facts.statement: Md. Habib Khan (21) of Nabakalas, Matlab Dakshin upazila, Chandpur, borrowed 5.5 lakh taka to go to Saudi Arabia in November 2023 on a 'free visa' through a broker named Md. Rashed from Narayanganj.
facts.source_in_article: family and local sources; father Mizanur Rahman Khan

facts.statement: Habib Khan worked for a while as a staff member at a residential hotel in Mecca, then left that job; afterwards, under a local broker in Saudi Arabia, he got only occasional small jobs with little pay and spent most of his time idle, so the 5.5 lakh taka loan was still unpaid at his death in October 2025.

Habib Khan suffered chest pain/heart attack about 12 days before his death, was admitted to a hospital in Mecca by a co-worker, and died there at 11 pm local time on Sunday (about 5 October 2025); his father says worry over lack of work made him ill.

As of early October 2025 Habib Khan's family was waiting for his body to be brought from Saudi Arabia; Matlab Dakshin police station OC Md. Saleh Ahammad said all help would be given to bring the body home.

headline_en: 38 people including children rescued from deep hills of Teknaf, two detained
summary_en: On Friday 3 October 2025 the Coast Guard and Navy rescued 38 people (18 women, 12 men, 8 children), mostly Rohingya, from hills near Kachchhapia Government Primary School in Baharchhara, Teknaf, who had been taken there to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea. Two trafficking gang members from Teknaf were detained. So far in 2025, 70 traffickers had been arrested and 239 people rescued in Teknaf.

facts.statement: On the morning of Friday 3 October 2025 the Coast Guard and Navy rescued 38 people (18 women, 12 men and 8 children), mostly Rohingya, from a hill area next to Kachchhapia Government Primary School in Baharchhara union, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, where they had been taken to be trafficked to Malaysia by sea.

Two members of the trafficking gang, residents of Teknaf upazila (names not known by 4 pm), were detained on 3 October 2025 and handed to police, to be sent to court on Saturday 4 October; legal action was in process.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Cdr Siam-ul-Haque, Coast Guard media officer; OC Abu Zayed Md. Najmun Noor, Teknaf Model police station

facts.statement: In 2025 up to 3 October, law enforcement arrested 70 members of human-trafficking gangs in Teknaf upazila and rescued 239 people including women and children; such cases rise in the winter season.

headline_en: Why nursing is a promising profession and what opportunities it offers
summary_en: Sabrina Mamata, a teaching assistant in graduate nursing at Bangladesh Medical University, writes on nursing careers. She says Bangladeshi nurses work in Europe, the US, Canada, Australia and the Middle East; nurses pass the NCLEX-RN to work in the US and the Prometric exam to work in Saudi Arabia and the Middle East, and demand for male nurses abroad is rising. She lists study options in Bangladesh and examples of Bangladeshi nurses in academic posts abroad.

facts.statement: According to nursing teacher Sabrina Mamata (September 2025), many Bangladeshi nurses work in the United States at high pay after passing the NCLEX-RN (National Council Licensure Examination for Registered Nurses).
facts.source_in_article: Sabrina Mamata, teaching assistant, graduate nursing, Bangladesh Medical University

facts.statement: According to Sabrina Mamata (September 2025), Bangladeshi nurses can get work in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere in the Middle East by taking the 'Prometric' exam.

The writer says demand for Bangladeshi nurses has risen in Europe, the United States, Canada, Australia and the Middle East because of a global shortage of skilled nurses, and that demand for male nurses abroad is increasing.

The writer says specialised nursing skills (intensive care, cardiac, child health, mental health, women's health, community health, neuroscience, nursing management) give an extra advantage in getting jobs abroad.

Bangladesh has over a hundred government and private nursing colleges; public options are under Dhaka, Chattogram, Rajshahi and Jashore universities and Bangladesh Medical University, offering diploma, BSc, post-basic BSc, MSc and PhD; a 'PhD in Nursing' has been started in Bangladesh with Korean support.
The Public Service Commission recently appointed 3,512 nurses to BCS nursing non-cader posts (reported September 2025).

Examples given of Bangladeshi nurses abroad: Nahida Akter (BSc Nursing, Dhaka Nursing College) did a nursing doctorate at Pennsylvania State University and works as a registered nurse in the US; Sadia Ivy (BSc, Sylhet Nursing College) teaches and researches at Hiroshima University, Japan; Ashikur Rahman is a graduate research assistant at the University of Alberta, Canada; Humayun Kabir is doing a PhD at McMaster University, Canada.

headline_en: Interim government re-announces old good news for students going abroad
summary_en: A post on the Chief Adviser's Facebook page on 23 August 2025 said Bangladesh has launched fully online certificate verification and an apostille system, with the foreign ministry issuing apostille certificates for public documents. The post claimed at least BDT 700 crore a year would be saved. Prothom Alo notes the electronic attestation system for education certificates existed before the interim government took office.

facts.statement: According to a post on the Chief Adviser's Facebook page on Saturday 23 August 2025, Bangladesh has launched a fully online certificate verification and apostille system, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs will issue apostille certificates to verify public documents, so students and citizens can have education certificates verified digitally without visiting embassies or foreign authorities.
The Chief Adviser's Facebook post (23 August 2025) claimed that verifying all certificates online for Bangladeshis' higher study and jobs abroad would save at least BDT 700 crore a year.

Prothom Alo notes that the electronic attestation of education certificates for applying to study abroad was introduced before the interim government took office; the 2025 announcement concerns making it simpler.

An apostille is a government-issued authentication stamp or certificate under an international system; a Bangladeshi who wants to use an education, birth or marriage certificate abroad for study, work or migration may need it apostilled.
The government says the online system removes trips to embassies, cuts fees linked to manual attestation, and reduces fake certificates and fraud in verification for study, jobs and migration abroad.

headline_en: India returns 22 Bangladeshis via Sylhet
summary_en: India handed back 22 Bangladeshis (17 men, 5 women) through the Tamabil land port in Gowainghat, Sylhet, on Friday 8 August 2025. They had entered India illegally at different times, were arrested by the BSF and Indian police and served prison terms in Tura jail, Meghalaya. After legal procedures they were handed to relatives.

facts.statement: On Friday 8 August 2025 at about 4 pm India returned 22 Bangladeshis (17 men, 5 women) through Tamabil land port, Gowainghat, Sylhet, in the presence of BGB, BSF and police of both countries; they were from Sylhet, Netrokona, Rajshahi, Mymensingh, Bogura, Jashore and Jamalpur.

The 22 had entered India illegally at different times, were arrested by the BSF and Indian police, and served various prison terms in Tura jail in Meghalaya state; Indian immigration handed them over following an application by Bangladeshi authorities.
After legal procedures at Tamabil, the 22 returnees from India were handed to their relatives, said SI Shamim Mia of Tamabil immigration police.

headline_en: Four teenagers missing together in Ramu; families suspect human traffickers
summary_en: Four related teenage boys (aged 14, 15, 15 and 16) from Mandalpara, Fatekharkul union, Ramu, Cox's Bazar, went missing on Friday 4 July 2025. Their families filed missing-person diaries at Ramu police station and suspect human traffickers or kidnappers. Police received a tip that they were in a house in Banglabazar, Jhilongja union, and were trying to rescue them.

facts.statement: Four related school and madrasa students aged 14, 15, 15 and 16 from Mandalpara, Fatekharkul union, Ramu, Cox's Bazar, left home between 10 am and 1:30 pm on Friday 4 July 2025 and had not been found by 11 am on Sunday 6 July; families suspect they fell into the hands of human traffickers or a kidnapping gang, or were lured by someone.

Taiyebur Rahman.

headline_en: From Raozan, Chattogram to real estate tycoon in Ajman; questions over source of money
summary_en: Prothom Alo investigates Jasim Uddin of Raozan, Chattogram, who built a real estate business (Yunus Real Estate, JR Residence) in Ajman, UAE, selling flats mostly to Bangladeshis; Bangladesh Bank has no record of him getting permission to send money abroad. The article explains the UAE golden visa (10-year renewable residence for about 2 million dirham investment) launched in 2019, describes the UAE as a hub of hundi, and gives remittance figures for Chattogram and Raozan. TIB's executive director says the money may have left through hundi or gold smuggling.

facts.statement: The UAE introduced the 'golden visa' in 2019 to attract wealthy foreigners: an investment of 2 million dirham (given as about 6.6 crore taka) brings a 10-year renewable residence permit with the right to live there with spouse, children and parents. Elsewhere the same article says an investment of 6.5 crore taka gets a 10-year renewable residence permit under the Middle East's new immigration policy, so the article gives two taka figures.

According to the article, the UAE keeps investors' information completely confidential, and the trend of Bangladeshis buying land and flats in Middle Eastern cities grew after the new policy took effect in 2019.

The article says the UAE is the destination to which the second-highest number of Bangladeshis have gone for work, and that Bangladeshi bankers consider the UAE one of the main hubs of hundi transactions.

EU Tax Observatory reported in 2023, based on data collected by the US-based Center for Advanced Defense Studies, that 459 Bangladeshis bought property in Dubai while concealing information; up to 2020 they owned 972 properties worth on paper USD 315 million (about 4,000 crore taka).

Bangladesh Bank executive director and spokesperson Arif Hossain Khan said in February 2025 that all permissions the bank has given to send money abroad were for business, and nobody has been allowed to buy a flat or house abroad.
According to Bangladesh Bank, Chattogram receives the most formal-channel remittance after Dhaka: USD 2.36 billion (236 crore dollars) in fiscal year 2023-24.

Raozan upazila, Chattogram, is among the top upazilas for remittance, with one or more members of each family abroad; it has 52 branches and sub-branches of 27 banks across 246 sq km (over 20 branches in Noapara bazar) for a population under 4 lakh. The article says it is widely known locally that many from Raozan abroad are involved in hundi and gold smuggling.
The article states that Islami Bank brings in the most remittance of any bank in Bangladesh.

Jasim Uddin of Raozan, Chattogram, once in the used car-parts trade in the Middle East and allegedly later in illegal gold sending to Bangladesh, invested heavily in Ajman real estate from about 2019 through Yunus Real Estate (owners Mohammad Jasim Uddin and Mohammad Yunus, agent no. 2978 on an Ajman government list) and JR Contracting; JR Residence flats (26 buildings seen in February 2023) were being sold for 1.5 to 2.5 million dirham (about 5 to 9 crore taka), mostly to Bangladeshis. Bangladesh Bank has no record of his permission to send money abroad.
facts.source_in_article: reporter; Yunus Real Estate staff; expatriate businessmen in Ajman and Dubai

facts.statement: Jasim Uddin's brother-in-law Ashraful Haque was sued in 2022 over smuggling more than 11.5 kg of gold and left the country after the case.

TIB executive director Iftekharuzzaman said such assets abroad may have been moved via hundi or gold smuggling, possibly fronting for someone powerful, and that the Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit could trace the source with help from the counterpart agency in the UAE.

headline_en: India pushing only Muslims into Bangladesh as 'foreigners'
summary_en: Translating an Al Jazeera report of 24 June 2025, Prothom Alo reports that most people India has pushed into Bangladesh since May 2025 are Bengali-speaking Muslim Indian citizens, many from Assam, held in Matia detention camp and forced across the border by the BSF. Assam's chief minister says over 300 have been pushed in since May and pushbacks will intensify; drives against alleged 'illegal Bangladeshis' have spread to Gujarat and Maharashtra. Bangladesh's High Commission in New Delhi says Dhaka sent a diplomatic note that the BSF's method does not follow international process.

facts.statement: Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said more than 300 Muslims had been pushed into Bangladesh since May 2025 and that such push-ins would be intensified (Al Jazeera, 24 June 2025).
facts.source_in_article: Himanta Biswa Sarma, via Al Jazeera

facts.statement: On 27 May 2025 the BSF took 13 people, including five women, from Matia detention camp (Goalpara district, Assam's largest camp for alleged 'illegal' migrants) to the India-Bangladesh border; they stood about 12 hours in knee-deep water in no man's land without food or shelter, BGB and local Bangladeshis refused to accept them as Indians, and the BSF threatened to shoot if they turned back and fired rubber bullets, according to detainee Ali; a Roumari journalist said the BSF fired four rounds in the air. The BSF denied this on 27 May, saying it only acted to stop illegal entry of Bangladeshis.
facts.source_in_article: detainee Ali; journalist Jiten Chandra Das; BSF statement

facts.statement: The Assam-based newspaper The Sentinel reported on 31 May 2025 that the BSF took back 65 suspected Indian citizens from the BGB; pushed-in people told Al Jazeera that at least 100 returned home on their own after BGB left them at the border (unverified).

Police in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, said they had identified more than 250 people they claim are 'Bangladeshi migrants' living there illegally, and their expulsion was in process, per officer Ajit Rajian quoted in local media (June 2025).
facts.source_in_article: Ahmedabad police officer Ajit Rajian, via local media

facts.statement: In May 2025 Maharashtra police detained seven Muslims as foreigners and handed them to the BSF to be pushed into Bangladesh; after West Bengal government intervention they were brought back from the border on 15 June 2025, said Trinamool legislator Samirul Islam, who said they were West Bengal residents and Indian citizens; Mamata Banerjee said on 16 June they were labelled Bangladeshi only for speaking Bangla.

The Assam government cites a 1950 law giving district commissioners power to expel certain undocumented migrants; Assam High Court lawyer Oliullah Laskar says it applies only to those who entered illegally or overstayed visas, not multi-generation residents with state-issued citizenship proof.

In a February 2025 Supreme Court hearing on 'declared foreigner' detainees, the Assam government said in an affidavit that detainees whose Bangladesh address is unknown cannot be deported until the other country verifies nationality and travel permits are arranged.
facts.source_in_article: unnamed local lawyer, via Al Jazeera

facts.statement: Assam sets 24 March 1971 as the cut-off: Bengali-speaking residents must prove arrival before that date to claim citizenship; Foreigners Tribunals can declare people foreigners over minor spelling mismatches in documents; the 2019 NRC final list excluded about 20 lakh residents, about 7 lakh of them Muslims; last year Assam told police not to refer non-Muslims (especially Hindus) who entered before 31 December 2014 (the CAA cut-off) to tribunals.

Bangladesh High Commission spokesperson in New Delhi Faisal Mahmud said Bangladesh sent India a diplomatic note that the BSF's way of pushing people to the Bangladesh border does not follow international process; India's foreign ministry did not reply to Al Jazeera by 24 June 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Faisal Mahmud, Bangladesh High Commission New Delhi

facts.statement: Mymensingh jail superintendent Amirul Islam told Al Jazeera on 16 June 2025 that another Indian citizen, Doijan Bibi, was in Bangladesh police custody; Al Jazeera confirmed the whereabouts of at least 10 people pushed into no man's land in May were still unknown.
facts.source_in_article: Amirul Islam, Mymensingh jail superintendent; Al Jazeera

headline_en: Number of Bangladeshi refugees worldwide rising for five years
summary_en: UNHCR data show that the number of Bangladeshis registering as refugees and seeking asylum abroad rose each year from 2020 to 2024: 28,473 registered as refugees and 108,131 sought asylum in 2024, mostly in Europe and the Americas. Officials and diplomats say most left for economic reasons and exploited political conditions, though some were genuinely persecuted. Experts link the trend to traffickers exploiting youths' urge to go abroad, including Mediterranean deaths and recruitment into the Russian army.

facts.statement: According to UNHCR statistics, 28,473 Bangladeshis registered with the UN as refugees in 2024 and 108,131 Bangladeshis sought political asylum in various countries in 2024.
UNHCR figures for Bangladeshis registering/applying as refugees: 16,780 in 2017, 21,022 in 2018, 22,766 in 2019, 18,948 in 2020, 22,672 in 2021, 23,935 in 2022, 24,126 in 2023 (and 28,473 in 2024).

UNHCR figures for Bangladeshis seeking political asylum abroad: 62,860 in 2018 and 62,860 in 2019 (the article prints the same figure for both years), 64,636 in 2020, 65,495 in 2021, 61,298 in 2022, 75,867 in 2023 (and 108,131 in 2024).

Bangladeshis registered as refugees or asylum seekers in the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Finland, Georgia, Cyprus, Bosnia, Australia, the US, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Papua New Guinea, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Hong Kong and New Zealand; in 2024 even 6 Bangladeshis registered as refugees in Somalia.

Government officials quoted say that claiming refugee status or political asylum requires a risk to life in one's home country; they say most Bangladeshi applicants in 2020-24 went to Europe and the Americas for a better life and exploited the political situation at home, though a portion were genuinely politically persecuted.

Diplomats say most Bangladeshis who left as asylum seekers or refugees did so for economic reasons, with reduced income during the COVID pandemic, shrinking legal migration channels, and political conflict in 2023 and 2024 driving the trend.

Experts say human-trafficking gangs exploit some young Bangladeshis' urge to go abroad by any means; deaths of Bangladeshis off the coasts of Libya, Tunisia and Italy in the Mediterranean have been regular for several years, and Bangladeshis are often rescued on Europe-bound trafficking routes.
The article reports that traffickers are taking Europe-bound Bangladeshis and forcing them to join Russian forces in the Ukraine-Russia war.

headline_en: India ready to send back 2,369 Bangladeshis: Jaiswal
summary_en: Indian foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on 22 May 2025 that India has a list of 2,369 Bangladeshis ready to be sent back, many of whom have completed jail terms and some of whom have waited since 2020 for Bangladesh to verify their nationality. He urged Bangladesh to speed verification. Bangladesh has written to India several times objecting to 'push-ins', which include many Rohingya.

facts.statement: India's foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Thursday 22 May 2025 that a list of 2,369 Bangladeshis living illegally in India is ready for return; many have completed their prison terms, and some have been waiting since 2020 (five years) for Bangladesh to verify their nationality.

Jaiswal said those living illegally in India, whatever their nationality, face action under local law and custom, and deportation of Bangladeshis requires Bangladesh to verify their citizenship; India asked Bangladesh to speed this up.

For some time up to May 2025 people, including many Rohingya, have been pushed into Bangladesh across various Indian border points; the Bangladesh government has written several letters to India condemning the 'push-ins' and asking India to stop.

headline_en: AB Party's 13-point proposal to solve problems of expatriate Bangladeshis
summary_en: On 21 May 2025 an AB Party (Amar Bangladesh Party) delegation led by general secretary Asaduzzaman Fuad gave Foreign Adviser Touhid Hossain a 13-point proposal on expatriates' problems. Proposals include passport renewal within seven days with courier delivery, ending the ESKL syndicate in Malaysia, online embassy appointments, published lists of Bangladeshis jailed abroad, a legal-aid centre with a 24/7 call centre, online verification of employer documents, blacklisting fraudulent companies and simpler paperwork for repatriating bodies.

facts.statement: On Wednesday 21 May 2025 an AB Party delegation led by general secretary Asaduzzaman Fuad handed Foreign Adviser Touhid Hossain a 13-point memorandum on problems of Bangladeshis living in over a hundred countries.

AB Party alleged corruption and a business 'syndicate' around ESKL (the passport service provider) in Malaysia and demanded it be stopped and services decentralised under High Commission control; it also demanded passport renewal within seven days with courier delivery.

AB Party proposals (21 May 2025) on embassy services: digital payments (QR code, online transfer, debit/credit cards); online appointment software at embassies to end appointment manipulation and fraud; more branch offices where expatriate populations are large; priority handling of labour complaints and active intervention in exposed labour exploitation.

AB Party proposed that an accurate list, number and updated status of Bangladeshis jailed abroad be published on the website with rapid repatriation, and that a legal-aid centre for expatriates (with a 24/7 call centre and simple online form) be launched by August 2025.

AB Party proposed an online system to verify employers' approval documents to control fraudulent labour-importing agents, embassy blacklisting of fraudulent companies, work with foreign governments to curb excess migration costs, an annual detailed financial report on welfare fund use (repatriation, legal aid, emergency help), and simpler documentation to cut delays in sending bodies home.

headline_en: Why 'push-in' from India to Bangladesh is unacceptable
summary_en: Writer and researcher Kallol Mustafa argues that India's mass push-ins of people into Bangladesh in May 2025 break bilateral border protocols and international law. He cites Prothom Alo figures of 167 people pushed in through five districts on 4-7 May and 78 left on a Sundarbans char on 9 May, including Bangladeshis who had lived in India for 20-25 years with Aadhaar cards. He lists the ICCPR, the Migrant Workers Convention and regional charters that bar collective expulsion without legal process.

facts.statement: According to Prothom Alo reports cited in the column, 167 people were pushed from India into Bangladesh through five districts between 4 and 7 May 2025: 73 at Khagrachhari, 46 at Kurigram, 23 at Sylhet, 15 at Moulvibazar and 10 at Chuadanga.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo reports cited by Kallol Mustafa

facts.statement: On 9 May 2025 the BSF left 78 people on Mandarbaria char in the western Sundarbans, Shyamnagar upazila; they fell ill after days without food, one had a broken arm and several had torture marks; victims said they were blindfolded and brought from Gujarat by plane and launch.

According to BGB, those pushed in from India in May 2025 include Indian, Myanmar and Bangladeshi nationals; many of the Bangladeshis had gone to India 20-25 years earlier, lived there with families and held Aadhaar cards and other documents, which Indian police or BSF kept before separating them from their families and pushing them into Bangladesh. Some Rohingya among them were registered refugees in Bangladesh camps and some held UNHCR India cards.
Bangladesh sent India a diplomatic letter on 9 May 2025 protesting the push-ins; reports said people were still being gathered at border points for push-in.

The column says a person who enters another country illegally must be returned under bilateral agreements and international law; India-Bangladesh border protocols include the 1975 Joint India-Bangladesh Guidelines for Border Authorities and the 2011 Coordinated Border Management Plan (CBMP), which designates BSF and BGB nodal officers to resolve illegal entry and trafficking issues by discussion.

Article 22 of the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families bars expelling migrant workers or their families without legal process and bars collective expulsion; each case must be examined individually. ICCPR Article 13 bars expelling lawfully present persons without due process, and Article 12(4) protects the right to enter one's own country; collective expulsion is also barred by ECHR Protocol 4 Art. 4, American Convention Art. 22(9), African Charter Art. 12(5) and Arab Charter Art. 26(1).
facts.source_in_article: Kallol Mustafa, citing OHCHR discussion paper 2006

facts.statement: The column says large push-ins from India were frequent around 2002-03 under the BJP-led NDA government and had not occurred on a large scale for a long time until 2025.

headline_en: Government will increase staff at Bangladesh missions: Foreign Adviser
summary_en: At a Foreign Service Day 2025 event in Dhaka, Foreign Adviser Touhid Hossain said the government is working to increase staff at missions abroad, especially consular posts. He said about 80 percent of migrant workers' problems originate in Bangladesh before departure and 20 percent in destination countries, and that missions serve over 1 crore expatriates. He noted about 32 lakh Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia are served by a mission of 50 officials.

facts.statement: Foreign Adviser Md. Touhid Hossain said at a Foreign Service Day 2025 event (18 April 2025) at the Foreign Service Academy, Dhaka, that the government has begun efforts to increase manpower at Bangladesh missions abroad, especially consular posts and consulate general offices, hoping for at least partial success.

Touhid Hossain said about 80 percent of the problems Bangladeshi migrant workers face arise from processes inside Bangladesh before migration and about 20 percent in the destination country, yet missions abroad are expected to solve 100 percent of them.

Touhid Hossain said about 32 lakh Bangladeshis live in Saudi Arabia, asking how 50 officials of a mission can handle the problems of so many; he said Bangladesh missions serve more than 1 crore expatriates worldwide despite limited staff and logistics.
Touhid Hossain urged mission officials to show more empathy, saying expatriates do not visit missions by choice but mostly come in desperation and in serious need of help.

headline_en: Will 1.5 crore expatriates be able to vote?
summary_en: Additional SP and Warwick PhD researcher Md. Imran Ahmmed argues that Bangladesh should let its over 1.5 crore expatriates vote, preferably online or by proxy, since postal ballots may not arrive in time. He notes official estimates of the number of expatriates differ widely and that expatriates sent USD 27 billion in 2024. He describes how the US, UK, France, Germany, Canada, Australia and Estonia let citizens abroad vote.

headline_en: Air ticket prices fall by 75 percent
summary_en: ATAB says Dhaka-Saudi Arabia air fares fell by up to 75 percent after government oversight: fares that reached BDT 1,90,000 due to 'group booking schemes' in December and February are now BDT 48,000-50,000, and as low as BDT 35,000 on Dammam and Riyadh routes with some airlines. The Civil Aviation and Tourism Ministry issued 10 directives on 11 February 2025, including mandatory passenger name, passport details and passport copy at booking, which forced airlines to release blocked seats.

facts.statement: According to the Association of Travel Agents of Bangladesh (ATAB), in March 2025 air tickets from Dhaka to Saudi Arabia cost BDT 48,000-50,000, and some airlines sold Dammam and Riyadh tickets for as little as BDT 35,000, a fall of up to 75 percent.

ATAB said that in December of last year and in February, Dhaka-to-Saudi fares rose abnormally, reaching up to BDT 1,90,000, especially because of 'group booking schemes' and artificial seat shortages (blocked seats).

On 11 February 2025 the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism issued 10 directives to stop abnormal air fare rises, aimed at transparency in ticket sales for Saudi-bound flights; passengers' name, passport details and a passport copy must now be submitted when booking, which forced airlines to release previously blocked tickets into the computer reservation system.

ATAB secretary general Afsia Jannat Saleh told BSS that government monitoring should be strengthened so airlines do not return to unregulated fare rises, and recommended more laws and restrictions to protect passengers, especially migrant workers.
ATAB held a press conference on 26 January 2025 urging the government to act quickly against ticket price hikes and the market syndicate.

The article says readers can check the Flight Expert website to find correct air ticket prices without hidden charges; Flight Expert founder and CEO Salman Bin Rashid Shah Sayeem welcomed the government measures.

headline_en: Climate migrants falling into slavery
summary_en: An IIED study published 18 February 2025, 'Exposed and Exploited: Climate Change, Migration and Modern Slavery in Bangladesh', surveyed 648 households in Pirojpur (Mathbaria) and Sylhet (Gowainghat) and found climate migrants falling into modern slavery in garment, brick kiln, construction and domestic work. It says households spend about BDT 461,220 (Pirojpur) and BDT 413,667 (Sylhet) to send a member abroad, financed by land sales or high-interest loans; most go to Gulf countries and a third work in risky construction, including Qatar World Cup building. The report recommends safe migration pathways, a migrant advice helpline and job registration.

facts.statement: According to the IIED study 'Exposed and Exploited: Climate Change, Migration and Modern Slavery in Bangladesh' (published 18 February 2025), a family in Pirojpur spends BDT 4,61,220 and a family in Sylhet BDT 4,13,667 to send a member abroad, raised by selling land or taking high-interest loans; migrants are often unaware of their rights and so easily cheated.

The IIED study says that between 2011 and 2024 many families from the study areas moved internally and also began going abroad, most of them to Gulf countries, and one third of those abroad work as construction workers in risky jobs, including on infrastructure for the 2022 Qatar World Cup.

The IIED study found climate risk raised households' likelihood of migrating within Bangladesh by 161 percent and of migrating abroad by 214 percent; it surveyed 648 households in 33 villages (10 unions of Mathbaria, Pirojpur and 9 unions of Gowainghat, Sylhet), with migrants in 70.06 percent of households.

The IIED study says Bangladeshi workers who built infrastructure for the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar were victims of modern slavery; it counts as modern slavery forced labour, forced marriage, sexual exploitation, inhumane work and housing, restricted movement, withheld wages, threats and beatings, confiscation of visas/passports for migrants abroad, and excessive or unpaid work.

The IIED study says international migrants are even more helpless than internal ones because they migrate on loans and returning home without repaying is nearly impossible; distance, high transport costs and the urge to support family make them endure abuse silently.

Jahangirnagar University economics professor Sharmind Neelormi said construction workers who go abroad have no option but to accept abuse and intolerable conditions; brick kiln and construction workers take advances (dadon) beforehand and must accept whatever wage the owner pays.

The IIED study says at least 92 percent of internal climate migrants become enslaved in some form; between 1960 and 2022 natural disasters in Bangladesh nearly doubled and losses quadrupled; average annual asset loss per household was USD 873 (BDT 1,07,379) in Pirojpur and USD 735 (BDT 90,405) in Sylhet; 69 percent of households reported house damage.

The IIED study made six recommendations: build local climate resilience, expand livelihoods, protect migrants from abuse, expand social protection, create safe migration pathways, and create financial security using climate finance; lead researcher Ritu Bharadwaj said the government should launch an advice helpline for migrants and a separate job registration system for them.

Shakirul Islam, chairman of Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP), who was involved in the IIED study, said families decide to send at least one member away when disasters leave no local work, but there is no protection system for these migrants.
